title: Current Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Surgical Planning for Craniosynostosis: A Scoping Review.
desc: [ANZ journal of surgery] Craniosynostosis, the premature fusion of cranial sutures, can cause abnormal skull shapes, neurological issues and aesthetic concerns. Surgical correction is standard, but planning is complex and operator-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers the potential to enhance diagnosis, optimise planning and predict postoperative outcomes. A scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines identified 11 studies involving paediatric patients with craniosynostosis. AI methods included unsupervised machine learning, convolutional neural networks, finite element models and variational autoencoders. Applications encompassed cranial severity scoring, phenotype classification, preoperative surgical simulation, intraoperative guidance and outcome prediction. AI-derived metrics correlated strongly with expert assessments, facilitated patient-specific planning and predicted postoperative aesthetics. AI is a transformative adjunct in craniosynostosis surgery. Clinically, it improves diagnostic accuracy, supports personalised surgical planning and guides intraoperative decision-making. Some studies show AI can contribute to better functional and aesthetic outcomes, showing great promise in the paediatric surgical field. Although AI does not replace clinical expertise, it enhances precision and reproducibility. Future research should prioritise prospective validation, integration into surgical workflows and development of interpretable, surgeon-friendly AI tools to maximise clinical benefit.

title: AI Chatbot Mobile App for Self-Management in Type 2 Diabetes
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Alexandria University; conditions: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 120; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Type 2 diabetes needs daily self-management, but most of it happens outside the clinic, where patients get little continuous support. Earlier studies of mobile applications and chatbots were mostly short, and few tested whether benefits last after use stops. This randomized controlled trial will test an Arabic-language mobile application with an artificial intelligence chatbot for adults with type 2 diabetes attending outpatient diabetes clinics in Egypt. The application offers diabetes education, reminders, glucose and activity logging, goal setting, prompts that adapt when use declines, a diabetes distress check, and nurse oversight. A total of 120 adults will be randomly assigned equally to usual care plus the application for 8 weeks, or to usual care with an educational leaflet. Outcome assessors will not know group assignment. The main outcome is self-efficacy. Other outcomes are self-care behaviors, medication adherence, disease knowledge, random blood glucose, diabetes distress, and application use, measured at the start, at 8 weeks, and 6 and 12 weeks after the intervention ends. About 20 intervention participants will then be interviewed about their experiences and what helps or hinders continued use, and these findings will be combined with the trial results.

title: Causally Constrained and Uncertainty-Aware Cardiopulmonary Risk Prediction
desc: Routine chest computed tomography (CT) captures pulmonary, cardiac, and vascular phenotypes that jointly stratify lung cancer and cardiovascular disease, the two leading causes of death in lung-screening populations. Yet clinical risk calculators evaluate each disease in isolation and omit CT findings, whereas unconstrained machine learning overfits small hospital cohorts, learns treatment- and illness-confounded risk directions, and conceals uncertainty when patient records are incomplete. Here we present the Causal Envelope Agent (CE-Agent), a two-stage framework that compiles peer-reviewed epidemiological evidence into explicit constraints on risk-factor weights before any outcome is seen, while estimating local baseline risk and newly added CT phenotypes from cohort data. At deployment, closed-form uncertainty propagation accounts for missing clinical or CT inputs within milliseconds per patient, running over two orders of magnitude faster than Monte Carlo sampling and returning calibrated risk intervals that direct chart review and selective imaging to borderline patients. Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, CE-Agent outperforms cardiovascular calculators in lung screening, exceeds the Pooled Cohort Equations on hard atherosclerotic events while correcting their 1.7-fold risk overestimation, and generalizes from a single hospital or CT scanner to external sites while lowering required sample sizes up to fivefold. Applied unchanged to lung cancer, CE-Agent matches established screening models with accurate calibration even when restricted to risk-factor directions alone, and pairing both predictions improves joint cardiopulmonary triage from a single screening visit.

title: LabARIA: A Multi-Agent System for Integrative Analytics in Clinical Laboratories
desc: Background Laboratory medicine underpins clinical decision-making across nearly every care setting. Clinical laboratory errors and delays can compromise diagnostic reliability and patient care. However, laboratory quality and operational data are commonly reviewed through separate manual workflows, limiting timely recognition of emerging problems across complementary data sources. Methods We developed and evaluated LabARIA (Laboratory Agentic Reasoning and Integrative Analytics), a multi-agent AI system for coordinated surveillance of specimen workflows, analytical quality control, and laboratory operations. We conducted a single-center retrospective system development and evaluation at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital/Weill Cornell Medical Center using laboratory data collected from May 1 through June 18, 2026, including 177,480 specimen-panel records, 75,103 internal quality-control (IQC) measurements, 633 proficiency-testing challenges, and 422 recalibration or maintenance actions. Forecasting agents were evaluated using patient-result streams with controlled perturbations, and synthetic staffing and inventory data. We assessed specimen rejection, cancellation, and turnaround-time patterns; warning recall and lead time before documented laboratory actions; assay-specific patient-based real-time quality control (PBRTQC) performance; and exploratory operational forecasting discrimination. Findings LabARIA characterized specimen and workflow patterns across clinical units and time periods, including hemolysis-related potassium rejections in the intensive care unit during early morning hours (49 of 367 tests [13.3%]). For analytical quality monitoring, the IQC agent generated warnings before 407 of 422 recorded QC actions (recall, 0.964 [95% CI, 0.942-0.978]), with a median lead time of 5.40 days (95% CI, 3.75-6.07). PBRTQC agent selected different monitoring strategies across 35 analytes. In a separate analysis, adding PBRTQC increased action recall from 0.964 to 0.993 (95% CI, 0.979-0.998). A dashboard presented tiered alerts for human review, and an accompanying chatbot supported interactive exploration of the summaries. For the operational forecasting module, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve for 7-day inventory and staffing risk forecasting were 0.800 (95% CI, 0.696-0.881) and 0.877 (95% CI, 0.778-0.950), respectively. Smart Technologies in the Management of Metabolic Syndrome and Oral Health: A Narrative Review.
desc: [Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland)] Background/Objectives: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) and periodontitis are two of the most common chronic conditions sharing an underlying mechanism represented by systemic inflammation. Smart technologies, including machine learning (ML), wearable and Internet of Things (IoT) devices, telemedicine and intraoral sensors, are increasingly used in both fields. This narrative review examined how these technologies are used to predict, monitor and manage MetS and oral diseases and what evidence supports combining oral and metabolic data. Methods: Following the SANRA framework, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for English-language articles published between January 2021 and May 2026. Of the 6922 records identified (3520 after de-duplication), 1852 were screened by title and abstract, and studies were selected by relevance to three research questions. Applications were classified by their current level of evidence. Results: ML models for MetS prediction often reported high discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] up to 0.99), but most were validated only internally, and several used the diagnostic components of MetS as predictors. Wearable, telemedicine and mobile interventions, usually combined with lifestyle programs, were associated with improvements in body weight, blood pressure and glycemic markers; artificial intelligence tools for dental imaging showed accuracy comparable to clinicians in mostly retrospective studies, with limited evidence on patient outcomes. Few studies combined oral and metabolic data: cross-sectional ML studies identified periodontal severity as a predictor of MetS and metabolic conditions as predictors of periodontitis, and salivary glucose correlated with blood glucose mainly in people living with diabetes, which does not establish diagnostic accuracy. No prospective study has tested an integrated dental-medical pathway. Conclusions: Integrating oral and metabolic data through smart technologies is biologically plausible and appears technically feasible, but its added diagnostic value, clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness have not been established. Externally validated models, prospective cohorts and trials of integrated care pathways are required before routine use.

title: Artificial Intelligence Assisted Innovative Low-cost Skin Testing Model to Accelerate Person-centered TB Prevention Services in Tanzania, Mozambique and Uganda
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: KNCV Tuberculosis Foundation; conditions: Tuberculosis Infection, Latent, Tuberculosis Prevention; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 1804; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] The Artificial Intelligence Assisted Innovative Low-cost Skin Testing Model to Accelerate Person-centered TB Prevention Services in Tanzania, Mozambique and Uganda (TEST4TPT) project will evaluate a person-centered approach to improve access to tuberculosis infection (TBI) testing and linkage to tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) in Mozambique, Tanzania, and Uganda. The project will generate evidence on the feasibility, acceptability, clinical utility, diagnostic and operational performance, and implementation of a novel point-of-care TBI testing approach, including home- or community-based testing and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted reading. By bringing testing closer to people at increased risk of tuberculosis (TB), TEST4TPT aims to reduce barriers to care, support timely TPT initiation, and contribute to improved completion of preventive treatment. The overall goal of TEST4TPT is to evaluate an integrated, home-based approach to TBI testing using SIILTIBCY (an authorized diagnostic skin test used to detect TBI), community health worker (CHW)-facilitated support, and AI-assisted result reading, with the aim of improving initiation and completion of TPT among close contacts of people newly diagnosed with pulmonary TB disease.

title: A thorough review on Deep Learning approaches to 2D-to-3D Registration in Medical Imaging
desc: 2D-to-3D image registration is a key component for several medical imaging purposes such as intraoperative guidance, enabling the alignment between preoperative 3D volumes and real-time 2D images. While conventional optimisation-based methods often struggle with non-convex objectives, sensitivity to initialisation, and high computational demands, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising alternative, offering improved alignment robustness and the potential for real-time performance. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of DL frameworks developed to address the challenges inherent in 2D-to-3D registration. We first outline how core concepts of DL are adapted to the registration problem. We then examine recent methodological advancements from multiple perspectives, including pipeline design, architectural innovations, and domain adaptation strategies. Particular attention is given to quantitative metrics, highlighting how performance is defined and measured across studies. Across the 41 included studies, we find that direct regression is the most common pipeline (23 studies, against 18 iterative ones), that hybrid CNN-attention architectures are gaining ground, and that research remains heavily concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration. We conclude by identifying the absence of per-case uncertainty estimation and the strong neglect of temporal or sequential modelling as the two methodological gaps most consequential for clinical readiness, and discuss state-space models as a way to add temporal memory within intraoperative latency budgets. Further opportunities lie in more principled domain adaptation and in the integration of foundation models for representation learning.

title: Effect of Data Preprocessing Decisions on Sepsis-3 Labels in MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD: A Sensitivity Analysis
desc: Objective: Published Sepsis-3 detection rates range from 3.4 % to 65.2 % in MIMIC-III and from 9.8 % to 47.9 % in eICU-CRD. We tested whether data preprocessing decisions alone produce differences of this magnitude when data, cohort and sepsis definition are held fixed. Materials and Methods: Using the MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD databases we developed and applied a configurable pipeline (medalabel) that stepwise maps the databases into the OMOP Common Data Model, standardizes and cleans the data, and preprocesses them to compute Sepsis-3 labels. Each setting of the preprocessing represents one decision of published Sepsis-3 implementations, and settings can be freely combined. On fixed cohorts of first ICU stays (13,388 in MIMIC-III, 94,782 in eICU-CRD), we changed one setting of a reference configuration at a time (51 variants in five preprocessing domains) and compared detection rates and septic stays (Jaccard index) with the reference. We approximately reconstructed six published pipelines and combined the settings with the largest effects in pairs to test whether their effects add up. The time a value is measured can differ from the time it is documented and thus available for automated analysis. Beyond the usual retrospective view based on measurement time, the pipeline optionally combines both time points to simulate a real-time system. Results: The reference configuration labelled 31.5 % of ICU stays in MIMIC-III and 8.2 % in eICU-CRD as septic. Changing a single setting resulted in sepsis detection rates of 15.3-58.6 % in MIMIC-III and 4.6-17.2 % in eICU-CRD. The largest shifts from the reference, all in the same direction in both databases, came from the SOFA baseline, up to +27.1 percentage points (pp) in MIMIC-III and +9.0 pp in eICU-CRD, from disabling imputation (-16.3 and -2.5 pp), the temporal window (+12.6 and +5.3 pp) and aggregation (-10.1 and -0.8 pp); clinician-validated parameter sets had little effect (-4.8 and -1.1 pp). Even variants that changed the rate by less than 2 pp labelled partly different patients, with Jaccard indices as low as 0.67 in MIMIC-III and 0.56 in eICU-CRD (1 = identical septic stays). Reconstructions deviated from the published rates by 2-10 pp. Two settings applied together deviated from the sum of their single effects by 0.9-11.8 pp in MIMIC-III and by up to 4.9 pp in eICU-CRD. Toward precision nanomedicine via artificial intelligence guided design and prediction.
desc: [Advanced drug delivery reviews] Artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing nanomedicine development by linking formulation variables and biological context with delivery, therapeutic efficacy, and safety. This review examines AI assisted formulation design, centralized formulation databases, prediction of nanoparticle self assembly, and models of cell and tissue selective delivery, biodistribution, and therapeutic outcomes. Recent advances in predicting nanotoxicity and nanoparticle induced immune responses further emphasize the importance of incorporating safety endpoints into nanomedicine optimization. Beyond nanocarrier engineering, foundation models and multimodal analyses of single-cell and spatial data are expanding biological discovery by characterizing disease associated cellular states, prioritizing therapeutic targets, and predicting treatment responses. Computational approaches also support the design of therapeutic RNA, peptides, proteins, and programmable protein nanomaterials. For example, mRNA sequences generated by GEMORNA and delivered via lipid nanoparticles increased erythropoietin expression in mice by up to 15-fold compared with a benchmark sequence. Integration of biological discovery with biomolecular and nanocarrier design may inform therapeutic cargo selection, targeting strategies, and functional nanomaterial development. AI may connect patient specific biological characteristics with predictions of nanomedicine delivery and therapeutic response to support patient stratification and individualized treatment selection. Integration of histological, imaging, molecular, and longitudinal data may enable treatment strategies to be adapted to differences in tissue characteristics, disease state, and therapeutic response. Emerging approaches based on digital twins and adaptive treatment control may extend the framework toward individualized dosing and dynamic treatment optimization. Major challenges include data heterogeneity, limited model generalizability, and the need for experimental and prospective validation. Progress toward precision therapy will require integrated frameworks that jointly consider delivery, efficacy, selectivity, and safety while clearly distinguishing demonstrated applications from future opportunities.

title: Interpretable distance-resolved graph learning for cancer gene priority screening
desc: Systematic screening for cancer genes (CGs) is still a central goal in precision oncology, yet integrating sparse and spatially dispersed oncogenic signals to identify testable candidates remains challenging. Here we present CGMap, an interpretable graph-learning framework that uses a width-oriented parallel architecture to prioritize potential CGs from biomolecular networks and trace mechanistic cues. By constructing distance-resolved channels, CGMap localizes spatially dispersed CG signals across multiple topological scales while avoiding representation homogenization. A global diffusion module quantifies gene cooperativity along pathway contexts and yields traceable virtual interactions that map predictions to potential regulatory hypotheses, providing intrinsic interpretability for model decisions. Across multiple biomolecular networks in a pan-cancer setting, CGMap analysed 12,022 genes, consistently outperformed existing methods while remaining computationally efficient and prioritized 70 reliable candidates, including those previously unannotated in established databases. Importantly, the prioritized candidates were associated with the suppression of tumour-related phenotypes, including reduced cell proliferation, migration and invasion, along with a shift of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-related features toward a non-mesenchymal state, as supported by parallel loss-of-function assays across cancer and non-malignant cell lines.

title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Stroke Registry Research: Current Progress, Challenges, and Future Directions.
desc: [Journal of neuroendovascular therapy] Registry-based studies provide real-world evidence that can support clinical decision-making, improve the quality of care, and advance understanding of disease. However, conducting registry-based studies requires substantial time and effort throughout the research workflow, including identifying clinical questions and gaps in existing knowledge, planning studies, developing protocols, collecting and analyzing data, and preparing manuscripts. This narrative review examines the challenges encountered in registry-based studies and discusses how artificial intelligence (AI) may help address them, based on evidence from the broader biomedical literature, with particular reference to our work involving the Japan Stroke Data Bank. AI, particularly large language models, which have advanced rapidly in recent years, has the potential to support literature searches, research question generation, and protocol development, although inaccurate outputs and fabricated references remain important concerns. Natural language processing may facilitate the extraction of structured information from electronic health records and reduce the burden of manual data collection. Machine learning approaches can identify complex relationships in large, high-dimensional datasets and may improve prediction, while large language models may assist with the selection of statistical methods, the generation of analytical code, and the interpretation of results. AI may also support manuscript preparation through language editing, drafting, and the creation of tables and figures. In the future, AI may make it technically feasible to automate much of the registry research workflow. Nevertheless, human oversight remains essential to verify accuracy, protect confidential information, and ensure transparency and accountability for research decisions and outputs. AI is reshaping traditional research processes and may facilitate the generation of novel research findings. However, AI should augment rather than replace the scientific and clinical judgment of researchers.

title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
desc: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. This demonstrates that loss-based scaling laws alone are insufficient to predict when zero-shot emergent capabilities become available. The capabilities reported here emerge after training at a 1:2,000 parameter-to-token ratio to accommodate the sparsity of paired biological interaction data. The same frozen representations achieve state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction at five orders of magnitude greater speed than co-folding methods. In prospective wet-lab validation across nine disease targets spanning seven protein families, Bonbon achieves a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds, yielding structurally novel molecules not previously reported to inhibit these proteins, including for out-of-distribution targets.

title: 3D Reconstruction and Generative AI in Undergraduate Urology Clerkship
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Nanchang University; conditions: Medical Education, Education; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 180; status: COMPLETED] This study examined whether a structured teaching program that combines three-dimensional reconstruction of kidney cases with generative artificial intelligence dialogue helps undergraduate medical students learn during their urology clerkship. One hundred and eighty students took part between September 2024 and January 2025. Students who received the combined program were compared with students who received conventional multimedia teaching. Both groups completed knowledge and clinical reasoning tests before and after teaching, and students in the combined group also completed satisfaction questionnaires. The study was registered after the teaching period had ended.

title: Future-Information Leakage in 30-Day Readmission Prediction: An Empirical Audit and a Calibrated Electronic Health Record Model in Medicare-Insured Adults
desc: Objective: To develop and internally validate a calibrated discharge model of 30-day within-system readmission in Medicare-insured adults, and to quantify how a future-information leak and outcome artifacts distorted performance, timing, and subgroup conclusions. Materials and Methods: Retrospective study of 236,906 Medicare-insured MIMIC-IV v3.1 admissions (87,750 patients; prevalence 21.4%). Predictors were audited for discharge-time availability; history features were tested for future information and recomputed from raw timestamps. A consensus gradient-boosted (XGBoost) model was selected inside patient-grouped folds; CIs used patient-cluster bootstrap. Results: A feature documented as a prior 180-day length-of-stay trend used each patient's whole record, including later admissions; removing it and two derived terms lowered test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from 0.774 to 0.706. The corrected procedure reached an out-of-fold AUROC of 0.7057 (95% CI 0.7016 to 0.7102; primary); the 44-feature model scored 0.7056 on the historically exposed test partition (calibration slope 0.99), above reconstructed LACE and HOSPITAL (both P<.001). A day-1 discrimination peak largely reflected 2,368 probable administrative continuations within 1 hour of discharge; merging these into the preceding stay gave test AUROC 0.698 (0.702 after refitting). The White minus Black AUROC difference was 0.003 (95% CI -0.018 to 0.024); specificity was lower for Black patients (0.61 vs 0.69). Discussion: Documentation audits and patient-grouped validation missed a leak that inflated discrimination and created spurious subgroup and calendar-period differences; simple empirical checks found it. Conclusion: Empirical leakage checks should accompany availability audits. The corrected model is calibrated, moderately discriminating, and needs external validation before clinical use.

title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework
desc: Patient-facing medical question answering with large language models (LLMs) is moving from research demonstrations to production deployments, yet evaluation remains anchored on factual correctness. Factuality is necessary but not sufficient: a response can be factually grounded and still issue a directive that, if acted on, would harm the patient. We introduce a risk-sensitive evaluation framework that scores responses by the presence and severity of six categories of risk-bearing language (treatment directives, contraindications, dosage expressions, urgency-triage cues, high-alert medication mentions, and overconfident assertions), anchored on published clinical harm taxonomies. Severity is classified by a three-judge LLM ensemble. title: Integrating Unsupervised Clustering with Transformer-Based Models for De Novo Cell Population Identification
desc: Single-cell transcriptome sequencing has been widely applied across the life sciences. It enables accurate and robust identification of cell types in heterogeneous biological tissues through unsupervised clustering, shallow learning, and deep learning. While deep learning does not outperform shallow learning in classification performance, it streamlines cell type identification by eliminating cumbersome preprocessing procedures. However, the availability of training datasets with comprehensive cell type annotations is always limited, so new datasets inevitably contain cell populations that are not pre-defined in the training data. To address this limitation, we integrated unsupervised clustering with transformer-based models to identify cell populations unrecognized by classical methods. Specifically, we developed the Nankai GeneRank Classifier by fine-tuning the pre-trained Geneformer-V1 model, and then clustered cells based on its softmax-normalized class probability matrix (SCPM). Applied to a public colorectal cancer dataset, the new method, named SCPM-based clustering, resolved cell populations that cannot be unambiguously identified by classical methods alone and led to the discovery of novel candidate markers of colorectal cancer stem cells, demonstrating its utility.

Implementing Artificial Intelligence in Daily Clinical Practice, from Voice Dictation to Operating Room Organization: A Targeted Narrative Review with Hysteroscopy as a Clinical Exemplar.
desc: [Journal of clinical medicine] Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering routine care through documentation tools, decision support, and hospital operations. The central question is whether these systems improve clinical work and patient care once embedded in routine workflows, not only whether they perform well on test data. This targeted narrative review follows AI from voice dictation and ambient documentation to operating room (OR) organization, using hysteroscopy as a clinical exemplar of the transition from technical performance to clinical utility. Evidence identified through targeted searches completed on 6 September 2026 was appraised with a framework that distinguishes image-level from patient-level results, internal from independent validation, and discrimination from clinical utility. Randomized trials and multisite observational data show modest, product-dependent benefits of clinician-reviewed ambient documentation; inaccuracies persist. Evidence for patient-message drafting derives from ratings of responses to public-forum questions and supports only bounded, supervised feasibility testing. In hysteroscopy, selected models discriminate well in narrowly defined tasks, but most studies are retrospective, image-level, or internally validated, and patient-level errors in high-risk categories are seldom reported. Reported gains in OR scheduling come largely from simulation. Safe implementation requires a defined clinical need, baseline measurement, subgroup-aware local validation, accountable review, and predefined criteria for expansion or withdrawal.

title: AI-Based Caries and Plaque Detection and Caries Risk Prediction in Children
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Marmara University; conditions: Dental Caries, Caries Risk, Dental Plaque; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 250; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This study aims to develop and evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI)-based system that can detect dental caries and dental plaque in children using intraoral digital scans and photographs, and use these findings to estimate each child's risk of developing dental caries. Children aged 4-13 years who attend Marmara University Faculty of Dentistry, Department of Pediatric Dentistry for routine dental care will be invited to participate. Participants will receive a clinical dental examination. Dental caries will be evaluated using standard clinical criteria, and dental plaque will be assessed using a plaque index. Intraoral photographs and three-dimensional digital scans of the teeth will also be obtained. Parents will complete a questionnaire about their child's toothbrushing habits, sugar consumption, fluoride use, dental visits, and selected sociodemographic factors. The collected digital images and scans will be used to train and test an AI model designed to automatically identify and measure areas of dental caries and plaque. The AI findings will then be combined with clinical examination results and oral health-related information to classify children as having low, moderate, or high caries risk. Based on the assigned caries risk level, individualized preventive recommendations such as oral hygiene instruction, dietary counseling, fluoride applications, professional plaque control, and follow-up visits will be provided. Participants will be followed according to their risk level and digital scans and clinical assessments will be repeated to evaluate changes in caries, plaque, and caries risk over time. The study is expected to provide information on whether AI-assisted digital imaging can support more objective, standardized and personalized caries risk assessment and preventive dental care in children.

title: Network scaling in swarm learning across real hospitals of different sizes: a KPI-driven analysis on the eICU Collaborative Research Database
desc: BackgroundDistributed learning lets hospitals train prediction models jointly without exchanging patient records, but how the benefits of a swarm network change as it grows, and which hospitals gain most, have so far been studied with artificial partitions of single-center databases. We examined network scaling on real hospitals that differ in size, volume and sepsis prevalence. MethodsWe applied the seven-KPI swarm-learning evaluation framework (Swarm Gain, Local Gain, Relative Local Gain, Model Stability Index, Jains index, Data Utility Index and label entropy) to progressive network scaling on the eICU Collaborative Research Database. From 25 hospitals (71,887 ICU stays; sepsis prevalence 16.6%), six hospitals stratified by bed size (two small, two medium, two large; 14,776 stays) formed networks of two, four and six hospitals in all six category-joining orders; four further hospitals served as substitutes in robustness checks. Swarm learning was simulated with the client-controlled workflow of NVIDIA FLARE (federated averaging, 30 rounds, five random seeds). The task was whole-stay sepsis classification from discretized vital-sign, laboratory and medication features with a 1,313-parameter feedforward network, with AUROC as the metric. ResultsNetwork AUROC increased with every addition in every ordering, from 0.734 (small-first), 0.755 (medium-first) and 0.781 (large-first) at two hospitals to 0.804 (SD 0.002) at six. Swarm Gain exceeded 1 at all nine unique transitions (mean 1.042 for 2[->] 4 and 1.020 for 4[->] 6 hospitals). Every hospital had Local Gain below 1; relative improvement over local training ranged from 4.1% for the strongest hospital (local AUROC 0.773) to 29.5% for the weakest (0.621), averaging 25.5% for small and 5.9% for large hospitals. Adding large hospitals gave existing members the largest gain (mean Relative Local Gain +6.2%); adding small hospitals never reduced it. Seed-to-seed variability fell from a coefficient of variation of 2.2% at two hospitals to 0.2% at six. Feature distributions were near-identical across hospitals (Data Utility Index 0.005-0.013), whereas the change in label entropy tracked Swarm Gain (r = 0.74). Substituting alternative medium or large hospitals left network AUROC between 0.790 and 0.805. title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
desc: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.
